group: Unit i — RRTS / High Speed Operations
title: Timetable, Traffic Regulation, Station Operations & OCC Functions

questions.q: Frequency of trains is calculated as:
questions.explain: Frequency (trains/hour) = 60 / headway (minutes).

questions.q: If headway is 5 minutes, the frequency is:
questions.explain: 60 / 5 = 12 trains per hour.

questions.q: If headway is 4 minutes, the frequency is:
questions.explain: 60 / 4 = 15 trains per hour.

questions.q: If headway is 6 minutes, the frequency is:
questions.explain: 60 / 6 = 10 trains per hour.

questions.q: If headway is 3 minutes, the frequency is:
questions.explain: 60 / 3 = 20 trains per hour — shorter headway means more trains.

questions.q: A shorter headway on a line requires:
options: Better signalling (moving block / European Train Control System (ETCS)) and disciplined dwell time
questions.explain: Trains can run closer only when signalling allows it and station dwell stays disciplined.

questions.q: A timetable is built from:
options: Running time + dwell time + margins/recovery time
questions.explain: The recovery margin is what lets a late train become on-time again.

questions.q: Dwell time is described as the biggest controllable cause of delay because:
options: Passenger boarding/alighting time varies and can stretch at every station
Trains are always late from the depot
questions.explain: Heavy boarding and door obstructions stretch dwell — hence Platform Screen Door (PSD) discipline and announcements matter.

questions.q: Dwell time increases most due to:
questions.explain: Passenger exchange is the biggest variable in dwell time.

questions.q: 'Regulation' of trains means:
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s live adjustment of the plan to restore even spacing and protect the overall service
questions.explain: Regulation = holding, short-turning, inserting a spare or cancelling a trip — live, by Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: Holding a train briefly at a station during regulation is done to:
questions.explain: A short hold re-creates an even headway so passengers further down get regular service.

questions.q: 'Short-turning' a train means:
options: Sending it to the depot for washing
Terminating it before its destination and turning it back to recover the timetable / fill a gap
questions.explain: Short-turning is a classic Operations Control Centre (OCC) tool for a late train — it restores service where the crowd is.

questions.q: During regulation, stops may be skipped:
options: Whenever the train is 1 minute late
Never, under any rule in any system
questions.explain: Skipping stops is a regulation tool but strictly only with authorisation.

questions.q: Inserting a spare train during the day is a regulation tool used to:
options: Fill a gap in service caused by a late or failed train
questions.explain: A spare train from the depot plugs the gap and protects the headway.

questions.q: Cancelling one trip can be the right regulation decision when it:
options: Saves the cost of one driver
Protects the overall service instead of letting one late train disturb the whole line
questions.explain: Regulation always prefers protecting the many over perfecting one train.

questions.q: The golden rule of regulation is:
options: Always run the late train first
Regulate for even headway, not just for the timetable clock — passengers feel gaps, not minutes
questions.explain: Two trains in 2 minutes then none for 18 is worse than one every 10 — even gaps are what passengers feel.

questions.q: Peak-hour service planning needs:
options: Maximum fleet deployment and minimum turnaround
questions.explain: Peak demand follows maximum trains out and fastest terminal turnaround.

questions.q: Off-peak service differs from peak mainly in:
options: Trains running without Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Lower frequency matched to lower demand
questions.explain: Frequency follows demand; safety and control rules stay the same.

questions.q: Which is a station operations duty?
options: Platform supervision and safe dispatch of trains
questions.explain: Station staff supervise platforms and dispatch trains safely, among many other duties.

questions.q: During a sudden crowd surge at a station, the Station Controller's correct FIRST action is:
options: Stop all trains on the line
Close the station without informing anyone
Regulate/control entry at the gates and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Control the inflow and keep Operations Control Centre (OCC) informed — platform overcrowding is the real danger.

questions.q: Which is part of station operations?
questions.explain: Announcements and information displays keep passengers moving correctly through the station.

questions.q: Automatic Fare Collection (AFC) gates and ticketing support at a station are handled as part of:
questions.explain: Station staff support Automatic Fare Collection (AFC) gates, ticketing, lost & found and amenity checks.

questions.q: Assistance to Divyangjan and priority passengers is the responsibility of:
options: No one — it is not a station duty
Station staff, as part of station operations
questions.explain: Priority-passenger assistance is an explicit station operations duty.

questions.q: The safe dispatch rule for a train at a platform is: it may depart only when
options: Train and Platform Screen Door (PSD) doors are closed and locked, the platform is clear in the dispatch zone, and departure authority exists
questions.explain: All three conditions — doors proved closed, platform clear, authority present — must hold before departure.

questions.q: Who owns the station and is its on-site commander in an emergency until relieved?
questions.explain: The Station Controller owns the station and commands on site in an emergency until relieved.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) stands for:
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) is the Operations Control Centre — the brain of the railway, working 24x7.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) supervises train running mainly through:
options: Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) screens showing train positions and signalling state
questions.explain: Controllers work with a complete line picture: Automatic Train Supervision (ATS), power state, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and radio.

questions.q: Which is an Operations Control Centre (OCC) function?
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) executes the timetable live and regulates trains when reality deviates from plan.

questions.q: During an incident, Operations Control Centre (OCC) is responsible for:
options: Only writing the next day's report
Incident management, decision-making and coordination with stations, trains, depots and emergency services
Handing everything to the nearest station without instructions
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) holds the full line picture, which is why its instructions override local wishes during incidents.

questions.q: Traction power control coordination in Operations Control Centre (OCC) is done with:
options: The Power Controller / Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)
questions.explain: The Power Controller works the traction power through Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA), coordinated by Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: Passenger information during disruptions is:
options: Given only after the incident ends
Approved/coordinated by Operations Control Centre (OCC) so all stations and trains say the same thing
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) approves passenger information so the whole line speaks with one voice.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) maintains which record of operations?
options: Event logging and reporting of instructions and incidents
questions.explain: Every Operations Control Centre (OCC) instruction is logged and recorded — vital for later analysis.

questions.q: In the Operations Control Centre (OCC), overall charge of a shift rests with:
questions.explain: Chief Controller has overall charge; Traffic and Power Controllers work within that coordination.

questions.q: The Traffic Controller in Operations Control Centre (OCC) mainly looks after:
options: Train regulation and Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) working
questions.explain: Traffic Controller = train movement; Power Controller = traction power.

questions.q: The Power Controller in Operations Control Centre (OCC) mainly looks after:
options: Traction power control through Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)
questions.explain: Power Controller handles the 25 kV traction supply picture for the line.

questions.q: Why do Operations Control Centre (OCC) instructions override a station's local wishes during an incident?
options: Because OCC staff are senior in age
Because OCC has the complete line picture — trains, signalling, power, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and radio
Because the rule book is kept only at OCC
questions.explain: Only Operations Control Centre (OCC) sees the whole network at once, so its decisions govern during incidents.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorises which of the following?
options: Degraded working, possessions, evacuations and emergency response
questions.explain: Major operational decisions — degraded working, possession, evacuation — are authorised by Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: A station's duties include checking amenities such as:
options: Lifts, escalators and lighting, plus cleanliness
questions.explain: Amenity checks (lifts, escalators, lighting) and cleanliness are daily station duties.

questions.q: Lost & found at a station is part of:
questions.explain: Lost & found is one of the listed station operations duties.

questions.q: Security coordination at a station is done by:
options: Station staff coordinating with security agencies, as part of station operations
questions.explain: Station operations includes security coordination alongside crowd and dispatch duties.

questions.q: The public timetable given to passengers differs from the working timetable because the public timetable:
options: Shows only the passenger-facing arrival and departure times, not internal operational timings
questions.explain: The working timetable carries extra internal detail — depot moves, time allowances, empty runs — while the public timetable shows only what a passenger needs.

questions.q: 'Recovery time' (slack) built into a timetable means:
options: Extra time deliberately added to running or turnaround time to absorb small delays
The lunch break of the crew
The time a train spends in the depot
questions.explain: A little planned slack lets a slightly late train regain its path without every following train becoming late.

questions.q: A 'clockface' timetable is one in which trains depart:
options: Only when the platform clock strikes twelve
At the same repeating minutes past every hour, making the pattern easy to remember
In order of their train numbers
questions.explain: Clockface timings — for example at 05, 20, 35 and 50 minutes past each hour — give passengers a simple, memorable, regular service.

questions.q: Holding a train for two extra minutes so that passengers from a delayed connecting service can board is an example of regulation done for:
options: Connectivity — protecting the passenger's onward journey
questions.explain: Regulation is not only about the clock; a short, deliberate hold can save hundreds of passengers a long wait for the next connection.

questions.q: A turnback (reversal) siding at a terminal station is provided so that a train can:
options: Change direction and start its return trip quickly without blocking the platform line for long
questions.explain: Turnback sidings let trains reverse clear of the platform, keeping terminal capacity high during frequent peak services.
